title: For 11 Winters I Secretly Shoveled the Neighborhood Grinch's Driveway, Then I Found Him Frozen on His Steps and Learned What He Had Hidden From Me
fb_text:
For 11 winters, I secretly shoveled the grumpiest old man's driveway before dawn. Two winters ago, I found him at 5 a.m. at the bottom of his steps on the ice, lips blue. When he died, his lawyer handed me an envelope. "I always knew it was you," it said. "And I never told you what I did either."

My name is Maggie Fennimore. I'm 52, and I work as a cashier at a pharmacy in Eau Claire, Wisconsin.

Eleven years ago, my husband, Conrad, died in a logging accident. He was only forty-one. We had two kids, ages eight and ten, and a mortgage I could never cover on a cashier's pay.

That first winter, I was barely holding on. Some nights I sat at the kitchen table with the bills spread out in front of me, too tired even to cry.

Across the street lived Mr. Horace Pickett. He was eighty-one then, a retired railroad man and a widower. Everyone on our street called him "the Grinch."

He yelled at kids who cut across his lawn. He phoned the city when my trash cans sat out too long. He called the police on my dog, twice, for barking.

He never waved. He never smiled.

That December, a huge storm dropped two feet of snow. At 5 a.m. I was out clearing my driveway before work, crying, because Conrad had always done it.

Then I looked across the street.

Mr. Pickett stood in his doorway in his bathrobe, staring at his buried driveway, gripping a shovel he could barely lift.

He turned around, went inside, and shut the door.

So I crossed the street and shoveled it.

I didn't knock. I didn't say a word. I just did it and slipped back home before sunrise.

When the next storm came, I did it again.

And the next.

For eleven winters.

He never mentioned it. Not once. He still yelled at my kids. He still complained about my mailbox. At a neighborhood meeting, he once called me "the woman with the yappy dog."

I kept shoveling. Maybe it was the only way I knew to keep Conrad's habit alive. Maybe it was just that no one should have to stand in a doorway looking at a wall of snow, alone.

Two winters ago, after an ice storm, I went over at 5 a.m. His porch light was on. His front door stood open.

Mr. Pickett was lying at the bottom of his front steps, on the ice. He had gone out for his newspaper and slipped.

His lips were blue. He'd been there almost an hour.

I called 911, then lay down beside him on the ice and wrapped my coat around him until the ambulance arrived. I didn't think about it. My body just knew what to do.

At the hospital, the doctor said he had a broken hip and hypothermia. "Another thirty minutes," she told me, "and he wouldn't have survived."

When he woke, I was sitting beside his bed.

He studied me for a long time.

"You," he said.

"Me," I said.

That was the entire conversation.

Three weeks later he went home with a walker. I kept shoveling. He kept not saying thank you. But now and then, when I got home from work, a bag of oranges sat on my porch. Or a bone for the dog.

This October, Mr. Pickett died in his sleep at ninety-two.

His nephew, Lyndon, flew in from Phoenix for the funeral. He'd visited maybe twice in ten years. He told everyone he'd be "taking care of the house."

A week later, a lawyer named Ms. Castellanos called me.

"Mrs. Fennimore? Mr. Pickett left something for you. He asked that it be opened in my office, with his nephew present."

When I walked in, Lyndon was already at the table, tapping his foot.

"What could he possibly leave you?" he asked. "You're the lady across the street."

"I shoveled his driveway," I said.

He laughed out loud.

"So that's how it works. You buttered up a lonely old man for a few years and figured you'd get the house. Let me be very clear. Whatever he left you, I'll fight it. He was ninety-two. He was senile. I'll sue you for every dime you've got."

Ms. Castellanos slid a sealed envelope across to me, my name on it in shaky handwriting.

Inside was one folded sheet. One line.

"Maggie. I always knew it was you. And I never told you what I did either."

Stapled beneath it was an old bank document.

From eleven years ago.

With my name on it.

The Winter Everything Fell Apart

She did it again after the next storm, and the next, for eleven winters. He never mentioned it. He still yelled at her kids and complained about her mailbox. At a neighborhood meeting, he once called her "the woman with the yappy dog."

She kept shoveling.

The Ice Storm

Two winters ago, after an ice storm, Maggie went over at 5 a.m. His porch light was on and his front door stood open. Mr. Pickett lay at the bottom of his steps on the ice. He had gone out for his newspaper and slipped. His lips were blue, and he had been there almost an hour.

"Me," she said.

That was the whole conversation. He went home three weeks later with a walker. She kept shoveling, and he kept not saying thank you. But now and then a bag of oranges appeared on her porch, or a bone for the dog.

The Envelope

This October, Mr. Pickett died in his sleep at ninety-two. His nephew, Lyndon, flew in from Phoenix for the funeral. He had visited maybe twice in ten years, yet he told everyone he would be "taking care of the house."

A week later, a lawyer named Ms. Castellanos called Maggie. Mr. Pickett had left something for her, to be opened in the lawyer's office with his nephew present.

Lyndon was already at the table, tapping his foot. "What could he possibly leave you? You're the lady across the street."

"I shoveled his driveway," Maggie said.

He laughed. "So you buttered up a lonely old man and figured you'd get the house. Whatever he left you, I'll fight it. He was ninety-two. He was senile. I'll sue you for every dime you've got."

Ms. Castellanos handed Maggie a sealed envelope, her name written in shaky handwriting. Inside was a single line: "Maggie. I always knew it was you. And I never told you what I did either."

Stapled beneath it was an old bank document from eleven years ago, with Maggie's name on it.

What He Never Told Her

Ms. Castellanos explained it calmly. The document was a record showing that the mortgage on Maggie's house had been paid off in full, eleven years earlier, during that first terrible winter. The payment had come from Mr. Pickett. He had asked the bank never to tell her.

Maggie sat frozen. For eleven years, she had believed a bank error or a quiet miracle had saved her home. She had never imagined it was the man across the street, who had watched her through his window and said nothing.

Lyndon went pale. He tried to speak, but Ms. Castellanos raised a hand. She told him Mr. Pickett had anticipated exactly this objection. Months before he died, he had met with her and a physician, and his clear mind was documented. His wishes were in order.

Mr. Pickett had left Maggie his house. In a note beside the will, he wrote that she had spent eleven winters clearing his path, and he wanted her children to have a place of their own someday.

Lyndon stood, stammered something about lawyers, and walked out. He did not fight it for long. The paperwork left him nothing to fight.

The Quiet After

Maggie drove home through the first flurries of the season and parked in her own driveway. Across the street, Mr. Pickett's porch was dark.

She cried then, the way she had on that first morning. But this time it was not only grief. For eleven years she had believed she was doing a kindness for a man who never noticed. All along, he had noticed. In his own gruff way, he had been shoveling her path too.

When the next storm comes, Maggie plans to be up at 5 a.m. anyway. Old habits are hard to break. And some kindnesses, it turns out, are never as unseen as they seem.
